summary:
Argentina's statutory framework remains among the most permissive in the world for legal gender recognition. Law 26.743, promulgated on 24 May 2012, allows a change of legal gender without surgery, hormone treatment or judicial approval, and the United Nations described it as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region. Argentina was the first Latin American country to legalise marriage equality, in 2010, and anti-discrimination protection exists through a combination of national and provincial laws.

Mendoza stands under that national framework, and no Mendoza-specific statute, enforcement series or incident pattern for transgender visitors is documented. That silence is not reassuring. Activists interviewed in April 2025 told the Washington Blade that police violence against trans and travesti sex workers has become more common under President Javier Milei, and explicitly worse in interior provinces without strong reporting infrastructure — the category Mendoza falls into, since this province sits under the national picture with no local reporting infrastructure to generate separate records.

The national security picture for trans and travesti people has sharply deteriorated. Per a March 2026 report by the LGBT news agency Agencia Presentes, drawing on the Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio, at least 227 attacks motivated by sexual orientation or gender identity were recorded in 2025 — up 62% year-on-year, the highest figure of the observatory's decade of operation, roughly one every 38 hours. Perpetrators were mostly security-force personnel and unidentified assailants in public space, with beatings the main modality. Institutional violence rose from 17 cases in 2024 to 64 in 2025, 32% of 2025 incidents took place in police stations or prisons, and 43% of perpetrators were strangers to their victims. A visitor stopped, detained or held by provincial police in Mendoza therefore enters the setting in which the largest documented share of 2025's recorded harm occurred.

Trans activists in Buenos Aires interviewed in April 2025, including representatives of organisations named for Diana Sacayán, killed in 2015, and for the activist Lohana Berkins, said the Milei government's policies had made the community more vulnerable to violence and described the situation as chaotic and desperate. Agencia Presentes described the 2025 tally as an inflection point in violence against LGBTIQ+ people in Argentina, with trans women bearing a disproportionate share of the harm.
tangentialFactors:
Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records negative assessments for same-sex relations, gender recognition and the registration of civil-society organisations, together with an assessment of deterioration against the earlier statutory position.

The judicial response to gender-motivated killing is contested. In April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán, while rejecting attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance that an appeals court had removed in 2020. The gender-motivated aggravation is therefore not currently applied in that line of cases, which weakens the deterrence available to a visitor facing targeted violence.

Mendoza's reported crime levels are not compared here with other Argentine provinces, and no source in the inventory benchmarks provincial policing in Mendoza against the national hate-crime tally. The national figures are drawn from an observatory whose coverage depends on media and civil-society reporting, so provinces with thin coverage register lower counts than provinces with dense coverage rather than necessarily being safer.
localsOnly:
Residents of Mendoza carry the full benefit of Law 26.743 for legal gender recognition: a change of legal gender is available without surgery, hormone treatment or judicial approval, on application before the national registry authorities.

That access has been narrowed by executive action. In February 2025 the government of President Javier Milei issued a decree modifying the Gender Identity Law as it applies to minors, and a second decree governing the housing of transgender people in prisons. Reuters reported that the decree bans gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy for adolescents. Legal experts interviewed by Agencia Presentes called the measure illegal and unconstitutional and a setback for the rights of adolescents, and signalled an intention to seek judicial intervention.

Employment and complaint machinery has also been rolled back: the 1% Trans Labor Quota hires were dismissed and the federal anti-discrimination agency INADI was abolished in 2024. Residents seeking to report discrimination therefore lost the national body that handled such complaints, with no Mendoza-specific replacement documented in the inventory.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Mendoza provincial statute on gender identity, hate crime or hate-crime aggravation is documented in this inventory; whether Mendoza has its own anti-discrimination instrument or a provincial equivalent to the abolished national agency is unresolved and not sourced here.

The claim that violence against trans and travesti sex workers is worse in interior provinces rests on activists' statements to the Washington Blade in April 2025 rather than on a province-by-province dataset, and no Mendoza-specific incident, arrest or police-use-of-force record is sourced.

The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio's 227 figure for 2025, its +62% year-on-year change and the institutional-violence breakdown (17 cases in 2024, 64 in 2025; 32% in police stations or prisons; 43% strangers) come from a single Agencia Presentes report of 19 March 2026; the observatory's methodology and provincial distribution are not detailed in the inventory.

Whether the February 2025 decree on minors has been challenged in court, and its current enforceability, remain unresolved: legal experts stated an intention to seek judicial intervention, with no outcome sourced. The same is true of any replacement function for INADI after its 2024 abolition.
